thought.text: Luck plays a far greater role in our lives than we realise.
thought.who: Amit Varma, distilling his years at the poker table into a lesson for life

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on poker, cricket and luck
lead.head: Don’t judge the shot by the six
body: Amit Varma was managing editor at Cricinfo and travelled with the cricket team before spending five years as a professional poker player. Only at the poker table, he said, did he understand cricket “for what it was”.
What poker taught him was expected value. With Ajay Shah, he applied it to cricket, and then to life itself.
Varma began with a fair coin. Heads, he pays you 51 paise; tails, you pay him 49. Over a hundred flips you should expect a rupee: one paisa a flip.
Take the bet, he said. Yet one flip loses half the time, and onlookers will call it a blunder. Even a hundred flips can leave you behind.
Shah had a phrase for this. “I always like to say, don’t judge a policy by an outcome.” Many a decision, he said, goes wrong “because of dumb luck”. {019-C01}
## Luck, not genius

Poker showed Varma how big luck is. Play Nadal at tennis a hundred times and you lose every game. The world’s best poker player against a beginner is closer to 51-49 a hand: skill needs a long sample to show. {019-C03}
“Luck plays a far greater role in our lives than we realise,” he said. Good luck, like where you were born, can make you arrogant; bad luck can make you defeatist. Sweat only what you can control.
Shah said this runs “exactly opposite to the great man theory”: the admired CEO may just have been in software in the right years.
## The new grammar

Then the hosts turned to cricket. A batsman skies the ball. If it goes for six he is brave; if he is caught he has let his country down. Varma’s point: the outcome alone cannot tell you if the shot was right.
T20, he argued, changed the game “in a very fundamental way, and no one noticed”: a one-day side has 11 resources for 50 overs, a T20 side the same 11 for 20.
With deliveries scarce, “the cost of a dot ball, a ball of which no run is scored, is much higher, and the value of a wicket is lower”. Aggression is worth more. {019-C06}
Teams nonetheless brought over the one-day grammar: pinch-hit, consolidate, slog. Varma’s answer, first set out in 2014, was to front-load: attack all the way and send the hitters in first.
A side that finished only two or three wickets down, whatever its score, had not been aggressive enough. “You left money on the table,” Shah said.

Varma also proposed a new yardstick: a batsman’s strike rate minus the rate his team needed to reach par. If it is negative, “the more runs he makes, the greater the liability he is to his team”. {019-C07}
## Easy on the judgment
Aggressive cricket, Varma added, is not always aggressive batting: facing an impossible target in Delhi in 2015, South Africa’s batsmen barely tried to score, and he thought them right.

His plea to fans: don’t rush to judgment. The probabilistic lens, he said, makes better fans and better lives: “we can stop being hard on ourselves for things that go wrong, and we can stop judging others all the time”.
He signed off by telling viewers that they had taken a gamble on the episode, and that by reaching the end they had shown “that the gamble was worth it”.

second.label: The coin toss
second.head: Heads you win, barely
second.deck: Ajay Shah on John von Neumann, and the edge hidden in a coin toss
body: A coin toss is supposed to be the purest 50-50 there is. Ajay Shah is not so sure.

When Einstein and others were debating probability in physics, the mathematician John von Neumann, “Johnny to all his good friends”, asked whether a coin toss was truly random or merely “our failure to compute”. {019-S05} Given some initial facts about a coin, his formulas predicted the outcome at about 0.66 to 0.33.

More recently, Shah recalled, researchers in a global project, which he thought was led by Persi Diaconis, tossed physical coins millions of times. A coin starting heads-up landed heads about 51 per cent of the time. Shah’s advice: to cheat at an important life decision, offer a coin toss. {019-J05}

quote.text: is the randomness of a coin toss something truly random about the world, or it is our failure to compute?

second.caption: the coin toss

third.head: Every career is a punt
body: You may think yourself too risk-averse ever to trade in the stock market. Ajay Shah’s reply: you are already speculating with your biggest asset. {019-S07}

Leaving college, Shah would put a question to people his age. Suppose you bought shares in a few industries for 30 years, betting on whether steel or software would do well. Everyone agreed that was speculative.

Yet choosing an industry or a workplace, he said, is the same bet, made with your human capital, an asset you cannot diversify. In the 1980s, who could have known that Indian pharma, or Indian software, would do so well? {#pharma}
By dumb luck, some people chose those careers and now look great. The media lionises them as geniuses. “Actually,” Shah said, “it is just the forces of luck in our life.”

sections.label: Expected value
sections.head: Right call, wrong outcome
sections.caption: expected value
body: Geeks, Amit Varma said, will call a decision “plus EV”. To explain what that means, he began not with cricket but with a coin, and promised to bring in Asimov and Clarke.
If someone offers you 51 paise for every heads and asks for 49 for every tails, accept. Your expected value is one paisa a throw. {#ev}
But the world judges by results. Lose one flip and people will point at you: “What a bad decision. You made such a blunder.”
## A universe for every flip

Here came the science fiction. Every flip, Varma said, splits the world into two parallel universes, heads and tails, and each splits again. Somewhere there is a universe with a hundred heads in a row. Which one you land in is pure luck.
So you cannot evaluate what you do by how it worked out, he argued; you can only live by a good set of rules. {019-C02}

Poker runs on the same sums. Facing an all-in of 100 rupees into a pot of 100, a player with a flush draw needs to win a third of the time just to break even. Add a gutshot straight draw and his chances rise to 42 per cent; now the call pays. {#flush}
~ So poker players are taught not to be results-oriented, Varma said. Ajay Shah’s version was shorter: don’t judge a policy by an outcome.

quote.text: After something has happened, it has hundred percent happened or zero percent happened. But before anything happens, it is probabilistic.

sections.label: Speculation
sections.head: Life above the API
sections.caption: life above the API
body: In polite company in India, Ajay Shah said, wise, stable, grown-up people are not supposed to speculate. He wants to rehabilitate the word.

Anything significant, he argued, involves judgment under uncertainty: a surgeon on a diagnostic pathway, a financier choosing where to put money, the two hosts deciding whether to build a new YouTube show. A worker on an assembly line, by contrast, lives a non-speculative life.
“If you wish to banish speculation from your life,” he said, “then you probably want a very dull life.” {019-C04}

Amit Varma had made a similar point earlier, citing his column *We Are All Gamblers*: choosing between real estate and other investments, or between software and television, is an implicit bet. {019-R09}
## Above and below
Shah then divided the world into those who live above the API and those who live below it. An Uber driver is told by code to take this customer from here to there. He has no agency. {019-C05}
Varma, risking expulsion from Shah’s circle of friends, asked bluntly what an API was. {019-J06}

An application programming interface, Shah explained: a function that takes an instruction and returns a predictable answer “time after time after time”. The designing, deciding and risk-taking happen above it.
~ “And we should all be above the API,” Varma said. Shah agreed, adding: “Most of us aren’t.”

quote.text: There are the people in the world who live above the API, and there are the people who live below the API.

sections.label: The skied shot
sections.head: Caught, or just unlucky?
sections.caption: the skied shot
body: As a cricket writer and editor, Amit Varma found writers and fans alike “too quick to pass judgment”.

Take a batsman who, at a crucial moment, tries to hit a six and skies it. Varma offered three outcomes: a six, a catch in the outfield, or a ball that hits a bird, falls on a fielder’s head and kills them both. The last, he allowed, is “incredibly unlikely”. {019-J07}
Caught, he is irresponsible; six, he is the brave hitter who rescued his side. Either way, Varma said, the result is no verdict on the decision.
## What football knows
Other sports have broken this down to a science. Football coaches know the expected value of a long shot against a pass to the striker, and drill it into their players.

When Pep Guardiola came to Manchester City, Varma said, he got rid of a goalkeeper good enough to play for England, because he could not play out from the back. {019-S06} Sometimes that style gifts the opponent the ball. “But on the whole it is plus EV.”
~ Cricket lacked such data, Varma argued, because almost every Test situation, such as a fourth-day dust bowl at Motera, is unique. The standardised T20 format changed that.

quote.text: this whole logic of play out from the back can look ridiculous, when you end up giving the ball away with a bad pass.

sections.label: Twenty overs
sections.head: Scarce balls, cheap wickets
sections.caption: the cost of a dot ball
body: In one-day cricket a side has 11 resources for 50 overs; in T20, the same 11 for 20. Amit Varma applied opportunity cost: with deliveries scarcer, a dot ball costs more and a wicket less. {019-C06}

That upends the old statistics. Averages and aggregates no longer matter, Varma said; strike rate does. A batsman who makes 900 runs in an IPL season, slower than his team needed, was “actually a disaster”. {#ninehundred}
Ajay Shah called this “the quintessential problem of all organisations”: a player’s urge to look good pulls against the team’s need to win.
## The hurdle rate
Judge batsmen by averages, Shah said, and you set them on the wrong trajectory. Judge them against a hurdle rate: what it takes to win.
The fix must go upstream to the selectors, Shah said: “It is possible to recruit a star trader in a dumb way, and it is the fault of the management that hired those star traders.” {019-C08}
Selectors, Varma added, often come from an older school, and find it safer to pick a man with a good average than one who correctly risks his wicket and gets unlucky.
~ The sums also shift during a match. Lose three wickets in the first over, Varma said, and the remaining wickets gain in value, so caution is worth more.

quote.text: It would have been better if he lasted two balls in each innings and didn’t waste time.

sections.label: The forecasters
sections.head: The certainty merchants
sections.caption: selling certainty
body: Amit Varma once planned a book on what poker taught him about thinking probabilistically. Then he read *Superforecasting*, by Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner, and decided his own book was not required. {#tetlock}

The book, he said, teaches the humility to keep updating your priors and examining your biases. Experts on TV and Twitter are incentivised to exude certainty, but in a complex world certainty is hard to come by.

Ajay Shah, as an economist, is constantly asked what the stock market or the exchange rate will do, and finds it “bracing to say, I don’t know”. Understanding finance, he said, means respecting its uncertainty. {019-C09}
## Seventy, twenty, ten

Pressed for an answer, Varma said, an honest forecaster gives probabilities: 70 per cent this, 20 per cent that. Those who gave Donald Trump a low chance in 2016 were castigated when he won, but they did not necessarily get it wrong. {#trump}
Shah finds the conversation between economists and the real world in India “a bit dysfunctional”, because people want a super-forecaster. Better, he said, to talk about the forces at work.
~ He recalled Churchill’s lament: one economist gives you two views, “and three if it’s John Maynard Keynes”. {019-J12}
~ Shah’s own pick, *Thinking Strategically* by Avinash Dixit and Barry Nalebuff, takes game theory in the sense of John von Neumann closer to real-world use. {#dixit}

quote.text: Understanding finance is learning to respect the uncertainty of that beast.

side.boxText: Amit Varma made the case in two pieces in 2016, *What Cricket Can Learn From Poker* and *What Cricket Can Learn From Economics*: one brings expected value to the game, the other opportunity cost. {019-R04}

contQuote.text: There is a universe of possibilities. There are so many parallel universes about to split up with every decision that you make. So you cannot evaluate anything that you do on the basis of how it worked out.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s betting tip, and why it worked so well
stories.head: The tip that called 13 of 14
body: By 2016 Amit Varma had retired from poker, but many poker players he knew dabbled in cricket betting. He says he never has, and does not advise it: “It is illegal in India, so kindly, gentle reader, don’t do it.”
Before that year’s IPL, one such friend came to him for a tip. Surely a man who understood cricket so well could see an edge.
Varma’s advice was a single line: always bet on the side batting second, whatever the price. The friend had expected something deep and nuanced. He ignored it. {019-S02}

After the 14th match he rang back. Had he listened, Varma told him, he would have made a lot of money. The chasing side had won 13 of the 14, easily, losing 3.4 wickets on average and finishing in around 17 overs. {#thirteen}

Chasing does carry a small edge, Varma said, because the side batting second knows exactly what it needs. But that is worth 55-45, or 60-40 at most. “Why was there this massive skew? Because teams were underestimating the par score.” {#skew}

The par score is the one that wins about half the time. Virat Kohli, then captaining Bangalore, lost at least three games in that run after batting first, Varma recalled, and implicitly blamed his bowlers: “we got the par score”. By Varma’s reckoning, they had fallen well short.
~ Teams were still thinking in an older paradigm, he said. That has since significantly corrected itself, “because obviously you live and learn”, but some still make the same errors.
stories.why: When the rules of a game change, players keep using the old mental model. That hands a big, systematic edge to anyone who has updated, enough for a one-line tip to beat any amount of nuance.
stories.postscript: Varma had written countless columns over ten years on T20’s changed grammar. They were, he said, “all completely ignored”. {#tenyears}

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s first poker column, and a lesson in nerve
stories.head: Fortune favours the bookworm
body: Amit Varma once wrote a poker column for the *Economic Times* called *Range Rover*. The first instalment was *The Bookshop Romeo*. {019-R10}
A young man whose favourite author is Milan Kundera walks into a bookshop. In a distant aisle he sees a pretty girl reading Kundera. Should he go up and introduce himself?

Suppose he is diffident, Varma said, and puts the chance of a date at 10 per cent and of a soulmate at 1 per cent. Those outcomes are worth so much, and a rejection costs so little, that the approach is “massively plus EV”. {019-S01}
~ Nobody in a bookshop actually does the sum. “You just intuitively know that I have nothing to lose,” Varma said, and the logic applies to every part of life, cricket included.
stories.why: Expected value is not only for gamblers. When the downside is a moment’s embarrassment and the upside a soulmate, the shot is worth taking every time, and naming the sum stops fear passing itself off as prudence.

stories.start: And a great example of a demonstration of how aggressive cricket doesn't always mean
stories.end: They c calculated that and they did the right thing
stories.caption: Amla and de Villiers
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the day two stroke-players stopped scoring
stories.head: Dead bat, live brain
body: On 6 December 2015, the fourth day of a Test in Delhi, South Africa went in needing about 431 runs to beat India, with a day and a half left. {#delhi}

They judged a win impossible on that pitch against those bowlers, Amit Varma said, so risk brought no reward. “Over here, there is no cost to a dot ball, and the value of a wicket is infinite.” {019-S03}
So Hashim Amla made 25 runs in about 244 balls, and AB de Villiers, one of the most aggressive batsmen of all time, made 43 in about 293. {#amla}
~ Onlookers could not believe natural stroke-players were batting like this. To Varma, they had calculated the expected value and done the right thing for their team, “even if it looked stupid”.
stories.why: Aggressive cricket is not always aggressive batting. The logic that demands attack in T20 demands total defence when risk earns nothing, and the right call can look foolish to an audience that judges by style.

stories.caption: the road to Bazball
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how cricket learnt to attack, slowly
stories.head: From 36 not out to Bazball
body: When one-day cricket arrived, teams played it like Tests, Amit Varma said. In the ’75 World Cup, Sunil Gavaskar batted all 60 overs for 36 not out. His defence: he didn’t play every ball. {#gavaskar}

Varma recalled New Zealand sending Mark Greatbatch in as a pinch-hitter at the ’91 World Cup, and Jayasuriya and Kaluwitharana attacking from the start in ’96. The middle overs stayed for consolidation. {#greatbatch}

About seven or eight years ago England began front-loading in ODIs. Scores of 300-plus became regular outside the subcontinent. {#threehundred} In 2019 they won the World Cup, with some luck in the final. {019-S04}

~ Under coach Brendan McCullum, known as Baz, they took this into Tests. Varma’s former Cricinfo colleague Andrew Miller coined “Bazball”; McCullum dislikes it: “It’s not just all crash and burn.” England’s real edge, Varma said, was expected value.

quote.text: they were the first to recognise that the ODI game for the last three decades had actually been played wrong.

quiz.q: What is Ajay Shah’s pithy rule for judging decisions made under uncertainty?
quiz.a: Don’t judge a policy by an outcome; judge it by expected value.

quiz.q: What did John von Neumann wonder about the randomness of a coin toss?
quiz.a: Whether it was truly random or merely our failure to compute.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s example, who lives below the API, and what does he lack?
quiz.a: The Uber driver, told by code where to take each customer; he has no agency.

quiz.q: Why does T20, by Amit Varma’s reasoning, make dot balls costlier and wickets cheaper?
quiz.a: The same 11 resources are spread over 20 overs instead of 50.

quiz.q: What one-line betting tip did Varma give a friend before the 2016 IPL?
quiz.a: Always bet on the side batting second, whatever the price.

quiz.q: Why did Pep Guardiola get rid of a goalkeeper good enough for England?
quiz.a: He couldn’t play out from the back, which Guardiola’s approach demanded.
